claims.text: An ab initio-trained machine-learning interatomic-potential framework can accurately determine melting temperature across near-equiatomic, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The framework can accurately determine enthalpy and entropy of fusion across near-equiatomic, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The framework can accurately determine volume change at melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across near-equiatomic, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The proposed framework is computationally efficient.
Local atomic structural fluctuations and short-range order/disorder transitions mediate melting in the targeted high-entropy alloys.
Machine-learning potentials trained on high-fidelity ab initio data accurately capture the complex interatomic interactions of high-entropy alloys.
Accurately captured interatomic interactions allow molecular-dynamics simulations to resolve the free-energy landscape relevant to melting.
Thermodynamic integration of the simulations quantifies latent heat, entropy change, and volume change during melting.
CALPHAD calibration can refine predictions by incorporating multiphase equilibria and compositional trends.
Predicted melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies, fusion entropies, and melting volume changes will typically agree with high-precision experiments within ±5–10%.
Traditional ab initio molecular dynamics is computationally expensive relative to the proposed framework.
Standalone experimental characterization can produce melting-temperature deviations exceeding ±50 K and fusion-property errors exceeding ±10%.
The methodology is most reliable for near-equiatomic, single-phase high-entropy alloys with moderate atomic-size mismatch.
Performance is less certain for alloys with significant phase separation, non-equilibrium microstructures, or extreme thermodynamic conditions.
Extreme compositional or structural anomalies may reduce accuracy because of limitations in training data and the need for model recalibration.
Deviation greater than ±10% across a statistically significant alloy set, or melting-temperature deviation greater than ±50 K, is specified as the result that would falsify the framework.
